item.title: NWS: Champi expected to pass over or near Guam Sunday morning as a Cat 2 or 3 typhoon
item.description: Emergency officials are warning residents of Guam and Rota to make “the full effort of preparing for a typhoon strike,” as Tropical Storm Champi approaches and continues to intensify. As of the 1 p.m. forecast, Champi was expected to pass over northern Guam as a Category 2 or 3 typhoon on Sunday morning.
item.content:encoded:
Emergency officials are warning residents of Guam and Rota to make “the full effort of preparing for a typhoon strike,” as Tropical Storm Champi approaches and continues to intensify.

As of the 1 p.m. forecast, Champi was expected to pass over northern Guam as a Category 2 or 3 typhoon on Sunday morning.

“This is not a very good outlook for Guam,” Landon Aydlett of the National Weather Service said during a media briefing Friday. Beyond the regular efforts of removing tents, canopies and tarps, Aydlett is advising people to use typhoon shutters and solidify emergency plans.

“Use the next 48 hours wisely,” he said. “Take action, plan, prepare, secure things, secure your homes, and make sure your family has a plan. If you need to be in safe shelter, find that safe shelter. Whether it's an evacuation shelter or with family and friends, make sure you're in a reinforced concrete home or building.”

Although fair weather is expected Saturday morning, conditions will begin deteriorating as the day goes on, Aydlett said.

At 1 p.m. Friday, Tropical Storm Champi was at 11.3 east latitude and 154.0 east longitude, or 590 miles east-southeast of Guam, and moving west at 24 mph.

Guam and Rota were placed under a typhoon warning, with typhoon-force winds of 74 mph or greater expected by Sunday morning.

A typhoon watch was in place for Saipan and Tinian. A flood watch was in effect for all four islands.

Guam Gov. Lou Leon Guerrero placed the island under Condition of Readiness 2.

“I urge everyone to take the necessary precautions and remain attentive to official emergency guidance,” she said. “Our island has faced powerful storms before, and we know that protecting our community requires all of us to do our part. I ask everyone to remain vigilant, look out for their neighbors, and follow the guidance of our emergency officials.”

item.title: Health Professional Licensing Office temporary closure Tuesday
item.description: The Department of Public Health and Social Services will temporarily close its Health Professional Licensing Office from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Tuesday. The closure will allow staff to facilitate the National Nurse Aide Assessment Program examinations, which are part of the certification process for individuals seeking to become Certified Nursing Assistants.
item.content:encoded:
The Department of Public Health and Social Services will temporarily close its Health Professional Licensing Office from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Tuesday.

The closure will allow staff to facilitate the National Nurse Aide Assessment Program examinations, which are part of the certification process for individuals seeking to become Certified Nursing Assistants.

HPLO services will be unavailable to the public during the closure. Regular office operations will resume at 8 a.m. Wednesday.

For more information, contact HPLO at hplo@dphss.guam.gov or visit guamhplo.org

item.title: Tropical Storm Champi track shifts to the south, passing over Guam
item.description: Tropical Storm Champi’s path has shifted to the south, with the current forecast track taking the storm directly over Guam. However, forecasters caution that the track could still shift.
item.content:encoded:
Tropical Storm Champi’s path has shifted to the south, with the current forecast track taking the storm directly over Guam.

However, forecasters caution that the track could still shift.

Champi is expected to intensify, likely becoming a Category 2 typhoon with winds over 100 mph when it passes through the Marianas this weekend.

As of 4 a.m. Friday, Champi was located at 11.6 degrees north latitude and 156.5 degrees east longitude, or about 800 miles east of Guam. The storm had winds of 40 mph, and it was headed west at 12 mph.

Guam, Rota, Tinian and Saipan are under a typhoon watch and a flood watch. Forecasters say damaging winds are likely late Saturday night and Sunday.

Residents are advised to pick up loose debris on their property, restock their emergency kits and gather any medications or other essentials in preparation for power outages.

item.title: Crowds throng New Delhi and wave Indian flags amid escalating protests

item.content:encoded:
NEW DELHI — Thousands of Indians thronged a bustling thoroughfare in the heart of the capital, waving the national flag and demanding the resignation of the country's election chief, the latest show of public dissent against Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government.

The protesters rallied in Connaught Place, one of New Delhi's busiest commercial districts, responding to a call by the youth "Cockroach" movement, whose leader Abhijeet Dipke was detained by police ahead of the demonstration. Protesters spanning generations joined the rally, reflecting broad public anger and intensifying pressure on the country's top election official.

Protests by the youth and opposition parties have intensified over an ongoing review of voter lists that has removed more than 130 million names since last year. Critics say the exercise is politically motivated, threatens to disenfranchise millions more, and has disproportionately affected minorities, particularly Muslims. They have demanded the resignation of election chief Gyanesh Kumar.

The Election Commission and Prime Minister Narendra Modi's administration deny the allegations and say the revision is intended to remove duplicate and ineligible entries.

Friday's protest was part of a growing campaign that has put Modi's government under pressure and comes a week after a police crackdown on protesters in New Delhi.

The demonstrators vastly outnumbered the security personnel lining the road, while columns of riot police stood watch.

Police had earlier asked people not to join the rally and offered to let a small group gather to wave the national flag and sing the national anthem. In anticipation of the protests, authorities also closed Central Park, a green space surrounded by Connaught Place's white colonial-era buildings, on Friday and Saturday.

Modi has not publicly commented on the protests. Some of his party leaders have dismissed the demonstrators as "anarchists" and suggested, without offering evidence, that they are backed by foreign powers.

Police detained Dipke, the founder of the "Cockroach" movement, ahead of the demonstrations. He had urged supporters unable to travel to New Delhi to raise the flag and demonstrate in their own communities.

A live video posted on the movement's Instagram account showed Dipke leaving a house and heading toward the street, where police officers intercepted him. After a brief exchange, officers hauled him into a police vehicle and drove away.

"Waving the tricolor (Indian flag) is not a crime," he told reporters Thursday.

The "Cockroach" movement began as an online satirical campaign this summer after India's chief justice compared unemployed young people to parasites. Many young Indians embraced the remark, adopting the cockroach as a symbol of resilience. It has since expanded into a nationwide protest movement of young people. Protests led by the group forced the resignation of Modi's education minister in July, a rare setback for the prime minister, who has been in power for more than 12 years.

It remains unclear whether the protests will grow into a wider political movement. Modi's government remains electorally strong, and anger over voter lists may not necessarily translate into support for the opposition, which has used the issue to criticize his Hindu nationalist government.

item.title: Sally Rooney's books will no longer be sold in U.K. after Palestinian Action support
item.description: Irish author Sally Rooney has long been described as "the voice of a generation" for her best-selling novels that are ostensibly about millennial relationships but also explore deeper questions of class, gender and politics. item.content:encoded:
Irish author Sally Rooney has long been described as "the voice of a generation" for her best-selling novels that are ostensibly about millennial relationships but also explore deeper questions of class, gender and politics.

Now the 35-year-old writer's books will no longer be sold in the UK because of her own closely-held political beliefs. She had promised to donate the revenues to a pro-Palestinian group that the UK has designated a terrorist organization.

In a statement this week, her publisher explained: "Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work. To sell a writer's work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher."

"As such, and in full agreement with Sally, we have taken the decision that we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format," Faber said.

The move comes after Rooney — who has said she believes Israel is committing genocide in Gaza — announced last year she would be donating funds from the proceeds of her books to Palestinian Action, which was controversially banned in the U.K. under terrorism legislation.

Israel vehemently denies allegations of genocide.

UK-based Palestinian Action says on its website it uses "disruptive tactics" to target "corporate enablers of the Israeli military-industrial complex and seeks to make it impossible for these companies to profit from the oppression of Palestinians."

It has targeted facilities linked to an Israeli weapons manufacturer and, in a major security breach, last year managed to break into Britain's largest air force base. The activists spray-painted two aircraft at the base blood red, in what the group said was a protest against Britain's military support for Israel.

Palestinian Action was also responsible for vandalizing one of President Trump's golf courses in Scotland in March last year, when activists painted the course with the words "Gaza is not 4 sale." Reacting on social media , Trump called those responsible "terrorists."

When the British government banned the group in July last year, it said it was on the grounds that Palestinian Action is responsible for "serious damage to property." It was the first time a terrorist designation had been given to an organization that does not call for violence against people.

"Its activity has increased in frequency and severity since the start of 2024 and its methods have become more aggressive, with its members demonstrating a willingness to use violence," the British government said at the time.

The government also said that the group's "activities meet the threshold of being concerned in terrorism as set out in the Terrorism Act 2000.," adding that it assessed "that Palestine Action commits and participates in acts of terrorism."

But critics questioned this assessment, saying it raised concerns about freedom of speech.

U.N. Human Rights Chief Volker Türk urged the U.K. government to rescind the decision, saying it "appears disproportionate and unnecessary."

"It limits the rights of many people involved with and supportive of Palestine Action who have not themselves engaged in any underlying criminal activity but rather exercised their rights to freedom of expression, peaceful assembly and association," Türk said.

Amnesty International UK also raised concerns, saying "the UK has a deeply flawed and overly broad definition of terrorism."

Under the U.K. law, anyone who provides financial assistance to the group could face up to 14 years in prison.

For fear of arrest, Rooney says she has stopped traveling from her home in Ireland to the U.K. to attend award ceremonies and other events since the law came into force.

But the novelist has defended her support of Palestinian Action, saying in an opinion piece in The Irish Times last year: "if this makes me a 'supporter of terror' under UK law, so be it."

It was in that op-ed that she announced she would use the British proceeds of her work "as well as my public platform generally, to go on supporting Palestine Action and direct action against genocide in whatever way I can."

Now however, her books won't be sold in Britain at all, so there will be no further proceeds.

The Normal People author was undeterred, saying in a statement shared with NPR: "I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions, and I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences."

Since the ban on Palestinian Action, several thousand people in the UK have been arrested for supporting them, mainly for carrying placards and wearing T-shirts.

The ban has been challenged in the courts, with the UK's high court ruling against it in February. A court of appeal later overturned that decision. Next month, the case heads to Britain's highest court.

In August, the U.S. Department of the Treasury followed the UK's lead in sanctioning Palestinian Action, calling them "far-left terrorists."

item.title: Do Americans own the president's papers? Appeals court to weigh in
item.description: President Trump has famously pushed the bounds of executive power since he returned to the White House. item.content:encoded:
President Trump has famously pushed the bounds of executive power since he returned to the White House. In arguments Friday before a federal appeals court in Washington, administration lawyers will make an especially bold claim: that papers created in the White House belong to Donald Trump, not to the American people. The move comes amid a series of actions under Trump's second term to test the limits put in place after the Watergate scandal, and could be another case that ends up at the conservative-leaning Supreme Court.

Six months ago, the Justice Department moved to invalidate the Presidential Records Act, a federal law in place since 1978. Conservative lawyer Michael Edney cast the move in a long line of other attempts to pare back statutes from that era.

"This is a story about a post-Watergate, overbroad statutory incursion into the prerogatives of the executive branch," Edney said in a recent webinar sponsored by the Federalist Society.

For some 200 years, presidents could decide for themselves what to do with the papers they created in office, until disputes with Richard Nixon prompted Congress to weigh in. Every president since then has complied with the records law, until this year.

"The Presidential Records Act is unconstitutional and a clear violation of the separation of powers," said White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis.

The White House's reinterpretation of the act comes after Trump was indicted on obstruction of justice charges for allegedly stockpiling classified documents in a bathroom, ballroom and office at his Mar-a-Lago resort. A federal judge threw out the case for technical reasons, related to the appointment of the prosecutor, and the Justice Department ultimately dropped the case after Trump won reelection.

Nikhel Sus is chief counsel for Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a watchdog group that sued over the Trump move.

"If the courts were to accept it, and we are hopeful that they will not, it would mean the people really have no right of access to the president's papers and that would be a major loss for archivists, historians and to the American people writ large," Sus said.

Senior U.S. District Judge John Bates, an appointee of former President George W. Bush , ruled against the Trump White House this year, in a decision that opened with a passage from George Orwell's dystopian novel 1984: "Who controls the past controls the future; who controls the present controls the past," the judge wrote.

Three judges from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit will consider the issue on Friday.

The Trump administration said in court papers that keeping all those records imposes a burden on the White House and that it could chill advisers from having honest conversations with the president.

But former government officials say being able to consult these papers is essential.

"Access to the records on national security issues of former presidents is really vital for the continuity of our government," said John Bellinger, who served as legal adviser to the National Security Council under George W. Bush.

Bellinger said he and other members of Bush's staff sometimes requested the papers of President Bill Clinton, to understand conversations Clinton had with world leaders and members of Congress.

"Often the only record of what a president has said to a foreign leader — or perhaps even more important, what a foreign leader, friend or foe, has said to the president of the United States — is in a written document," Bellinger said.

To not be able to see those papers, he said, will leave future presidents at a "terrible disadvantage."

Edney, who also worked for Bush's National Security Council and Justice Department, said he believed that Congress could probably pass a "thoughtful" records preservation statute. He said parts of the current Presidential Records Act that provide Congress with automatic access and presume the records will be publicly disclosed are "constitutionally problematic."

Edney said he has some doubts about whether the watchdog groups suing to challenge Trump's move actually have legal standing to proceed.

But the Trump administration appears to have breezed past those concerns, because they have a higher goal in mind.

"They want this to go to the Supreme Court," Edney said. "I think they want this resolved at a time of their choosing, with arguments of their choosing, and a court of their choosing, and with the Solicitor General's office that's making their arguments, as opposed to a subsequent administration."
